notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00454.opp-gr: The text has lacunae at the opening of §1, in §16 and in §17, marked by the edition with dots; the sentences around them are incomplete. In §2 an apparatus siglum list from the printed page has crept into the text and has been omitted. In §5 the text is partly restored, and ρωθεν is presumably ἑκατέρωθεν. In §12 προσείων assumes the restored reading; in §14 'κερδαίνοι αἶνοι' looks like a dittography and has been read as κερδαίνοι. In §15 'ἔκειτο' is taken to mean 'it had been paid', which is uncertain. In §17 'πρὸς δὲ τοῖς ποσὶν ἄργυρον τοῦ παιδαγωγοῦ' is obscure. Cimon is Libanius' son (Arabius).

17.2: kotyle is a small liquid measure. 20.1: the opening clause (ἔδειξε δὲ οἷς ἄφωνος τὸ λυπήσειν εἶπε) is obscure and may be corrupt; rendered by sense. The 'tyrant' is unidentified (perhaps the usurper Procopius). 21.2: Lucianus is apparently an official or rival of Eustathius; the chariot liturgy is the provision of chariot races. 28.2: 'the more august one' is taken as a higher council (probably the Senate of Constantinople).

36.1: 'Μουσήλιος' is evidently a corruption; 'Musonius' is a conjectural reading and uncertain. 37.1: the last sentence is obscure, and 'ὁ τότε τότε εἰπὼν' looks corrupt; I translated the probable sense. 'Γῶν' (37.1, 38) is read as 'τῶν'. 43.1: 'ἴνα δὲ σφῶν ὑποθεὶς' is corrupt; the sense 'laying them out' is a guess, and '[my eyes]' is supplied. 38: 'ἴστων' is read as 'ἵστη'. 46: 'ἐπ᾽ ἀμυθήτοις' is uncertain; it may conceal 'ἐπ᾽ ἀμνηστίᾳ'. 47: the closing sentences are ironic, putting the governor's pretexts in his mouth.

50: ἀσελγαίνοιεν γράμμασιν ('behaved outrageously in letters') is obscure; the reference of the clause about the guards and bandits at the end is also uncertain, and the text may be corrupt. 51: ὧν οὐ δεῖν καθαρὰ τηρεῖν is difficult; taken as Eustathius' claim that councillors' bodies need not be exempt from such blows, but the negative may be corrupt. 52: 'no less worthy to be called a sophist' lacks a stated comparison in the text. 59: the text is broken at δοκούν- νομίζειν (words lost), marked [...]; the duplicated supplement <τὰ τῶν φίλων, ἀλλ'> was read once. 64: ἀλλ' ἔχων] appears to be a bracketed deletion and was not translated twice. 'Leader of the Muses' renders Μουσηγέτης (Apollo).

70: καρπὸς πατρῴας πονηραῖς is corrupt as printed; translated as if πατρῴας πονηρίας ('of inherited wickedness'). 'Of no account' renders the quoted ἐν οὐδενί, apparently proverbial. 71: ἀκήλασε read as ἀπήλασε. 73: ἄων read as ᾄδων, ἀρειμένων as ἀφειμένων. 74: the clause καὶ ταῦτα πολλοῦ χρόνου ... ἐπεγειρόντων is syntactically difficult; rendering uncertain. πεφθλαγμένον is corrupt; 'neglected' is a guess from context. 75: οὐκ ἐροίην ('I would not speak/deliver them') is uncertain; some may emend to a verb of refusing, which would reverse the sense. 76: ἵρως read as ἔρως, ὦσεν ὲν as ὦσεν. 80: 'the horn' (τὸ κέρας) is obscure; possibly corrupt for κέρδος or an allusion I could not identify. ἄων again read as ᾄδων. 81: αἰκισομένων ('meant to torment') uncertain; ἴδει read as ἔδει.

nodes.text: LIV.
TO EUSTATHIUS, ON THE HONOURS.

[...] Since I have spoken about these matters not badly, as I at least persuade myself, come, let me also go through what sort of man he has proved towards me in other respects, and persuade these excellent advocates, who are indeed my friends, that I have been slighted rather than that I have done this.

I shall go back a little. I do not speak of the whole period, but of the one that received the cares concerning the imperial revenue. In this period, then, he devoted his nights to those [cares], but divided the day between that same [business] and my company. And there were times when he allotted more to this, composing and putting together speeches, making me their judge, and being praised. For I did praise [him], so that he might go away more pleased rather than pained. For I thought that from such [treatment] he would advance to something finer.

But he, in return for this, kissing my knees, and praying to see his son among my pupils, and saying that, if he should obtain this office which he holds, for there were in fact hopes, for those in the know, from what he had given, of obtaining it, saying, then, [that there would be] extravagant honours which he would employ towards me, and that he would show up as small everything [done] before, and that those who had held office earlier [were] experts at honouring a sophist, what did he do once he was in office?

In Phoenicia, to Olympius, this was constantly [on his lips] every day: 'Shall I ever see that man? Shall I say something to him? Shall I hear him speak? He will spend little time at home, and most of it he will be with me, if I persuade him to this, or even compel him.' And there was nothing in his mouth so much as I. And Olympius, on returning, reported this. Which also made many come to me, so that, if they should later need anything from the governor, they might obtain it through me, being able to remind [him] of what they had done for me.

And while there was an expectation that I would be summoned by him, through the couriers meeting one another, some arriving, others returning, and carrying messages from each side to each, such were the hopes; but I have been summoned through no courier up to this day, neither at the beginning of the day nor at midday, not in the late afternoon, not at the lighting of the lamps.

Nor have we spent any part of the night in talk, neither serious nor playful. But these things [he does] with so-and-so and so-and-so every day. And if [people] often come in while he is doing his own business, that is at once thrown aside and lies on the ground, and they fill his ears with unjust talk, provoking him against decent people and making him well disposed to those who deserve punishment.

But the greatest thing, in which one could best observe the insult: I have a son who is modest, and who has not lost this through practising as an advocate, but who, while no poor speaker, gets less than those who do not know how [to speak]. This [son] this man both knew and praised, and promised to make him distinguished if he should take over this seat. We thought, then, that once he had taken it over he would both make good his promises and call him at once and give him right of entry, and order the chief of his staff to admit him, and tell all the orators that he would wish each of them to assist [him] as far as he could, and that this should become a matter of rivalry among them.

But he [did] nothing of the kind, neither greater nor less. And yet he ought, when writing to me, to have put the man somewhere in the letter, or, if not that, after it to have bidden [me] greet [him], and, when he did not appear among those who came to meet him, to have looked for him, and again, when he did not appear in the courts, to have looked for him. Or was it much trouble to say 'Where is so-and-so?' But not even to me myself afterwards [did he say] any such word.

I, for my part, expected that, with everyone hearing, my son would be called inside, and that once he had come in, at a second summons through him, he would sit close to him and would lunch and dine with him. For this would not have arisen from any obligation to entertain all the advocates, nor from his skill, but from [the obligation] towards me of the man who said he would honour [me], his promises having done this as no one else's had, so that no one should wonder if I, who had not thought fit to have this from anyone else, now expected it.

'And yet,' he says, 'I sent and asked what prevented him from doing the advocate's work.' Not you yourself, at any rate, did you send. How could you? You did not even have his name in your mind, and it was not your doing, that not-your-doing. For how [could it be] yours, what you did not even think of? It is clear from this: having already come through many days and cases and affairs, you did not ask this, having omitted to ask about the one who did not appear; but some man, ashamed for the teacher at the wrongs you were doing, told [you] that you must send and inquire about this, and that he would not leave you unless you did so. So you sent unwillingly, and this is the way of those under compulsion.

That this is how things are, you are witness against yourself. For when he did not respond, having some excuse from his body too, but discouragement mostly causing it, you could not name a second inquiry about the same matter through a second man.

'And yet,' he says, 'I also summoned him by letter, holding out, like an olive branch, the gold from the cases, and at the same time asking whether more coming his way from elsewhere was the cause of the fee from here being disdained.' Well, I have the same argument here too, carrying its refutation with equal force. For this letter too was not the work of the man who sent it, but of the man who persuaded him to send it.

And who was he? It was Heraclius the orator, who had married into that man's family, and who saw us neglected, and the neglect putting the neglecter in disrepute. Having talked, then, to someone of the household, and mentioned the number of those who blamed the affair, and that he would have no answer to those making the charge, he forced out of him these small words.

And what followed again confirms what I said, that it was Heraclius who wrote. For when Cimon did not respond, though he could have learned how this had come about, he showed neither grief nor anger, nor that he would not tolerate a feigned illness. Yet he should have called doctors and sent them to the man, and inquired whether he had withdrawn from the courts willingly or unwillingly. And it would have been fine, I think, both to cry out against him and to threaten him and [come] near to blows. For by threatening, the friend would have shown himself in each [of these], and the one who was frightened would, from these very things, have rejoiced, seeing the goodwill of the judge in what had alarmed him. But, I think, in summoning he prayed that the summons would be in vain and that those sent would come back with nothing done, so that by summoning he might seem kind, and by the second [refusal] also gain not seeing the one he did not even want [to see].

Further, then, when taxes were being mentioned, and the clerk said that Cimon owed something, lying, for it had been paid, at any rate when he had spoken the name, and such compulsion had arisen to say 'Where is this man? And how is it that he does not defend litigants?', he did not judge him worthy of a word but went on to something else. So intently did he consider what he might do to please me.

And why need one wonder if we have suffered this in the matter of taxes? For yesterday, saying that he was grateful to me for his son, since in not many days he had made much progress [...], not to see my son in his own son, nor, in what had come to that one from me, the nothing [that came] to this one from himself, thinking it right that his own affairs should fare better through mine, but mine worse through his.

To such a pitch of justice has our judge come. He could not even say this: 'You have, my good man, payment for your labours over his speeches, since my son put staters into your hand, and the attendant silver at your feet.' And yet we know of countless teachers who have received fees for their sons from many governors, to the pleasure of the givers, who, naturally, often prayed in the temples that the time would come which would bring them this expense. But he, instead of compelling [me] to take even if I avoided taking, [...] thinking it right to enjoy this too from his office.

But if not gold or silver, did he send me something of what is harvested in the land of the Tyrians, and enslave me by that? No, not even a *kotyle* [a small measure] of wine or of oil. So he could not take refuge in the claim that he no longer owes me anything because he has paid a fee.

But the whole thing is an old hatred, hidden for the rest of the time but revealed in the time of his office. Otherwise, why did he not reproach me for not coming to him at the same intervals of days as I go to the others, nor say: 'You do wrong not to visit us often, but to treat me as you treat those who are nothing like me, at least in their dealings with you'? He said nothing of the kind, but he would gladly have said, had it been allowed, 'It is better for you, old man, to stay at home than to bestir yourself like this.'

And he showed by what he did, without a word, that he meant to hurt me. For he brought the gift of the staters to the poet who had insulted our chorus in his verses, conferring the same favours on him again after the tyrant; and over the very verses which he knew were most ill spoken of, he claimed that the man had outdone himself, looking at me alone among so many who sat beside him, challenging me to a contest as if he would throw me at once.

Then the man who had said he very much wanted to say something to me about many matters and to hear [from me] with nobody present, when I stood up as if to leave, all but pushed me out, by his posture, his look and the words suited to such a moment, thinking the small delay of my arranging my cloak properly a long one. So he was glad to see me go, while those who help him in what he wants sat on, this man who used to say in Phoenicia that he very much wanted to see our city, not in order to enjoy its other attractions, but in order to enjoy me.

This too comes from the same spirit. Someone mentioned Julian, a man who was one of those who had undertaken the heavy liturgy, the one involving the chariots, and who had sold the only farm he had and plunged his father, a very old man who had reached a hundred years, into continual lamentation. This Julian, then, when someone said that he was carrying the decisions of the judge to Lucianus, he handed over to prison without summoning him, without examining the charge, without waiting for proof, without giving him opportunity for a defence, but thinking it enough that one of the man's enemies had said that he was doing wrong. Then, having bound him, he left him bound, and neither the passing of a great part of the day, nor the coming of night, nor its end, nor the addition of a second day, stopped the evil, and this although a man familiar to him and above suspicion wrote again and again advising him to cease from what he ought never even to have begun.

To appearance, then, one person was wronged, but in truth, along with that person, the laws. They require that judgement follow charges, and penalty follow proof, when the prosecutor's case prevails over the defendant's. But here it did not prevail. For how could it, over what had not even been spoken? And how could the absent man have spoken? Would he then, if present and ordered to keep silent, have been wronged, but, being absent, have been convicted?

Let us consider also the very measure of the punishment. Imprisonment was the punishment, and you could have seen him lying in the midst of those who had committed the most dreadful crimes, perishing from the stench coming from them and from the clanking of the chains, weeping himself and hearing from his family about his wife's wailing. For a shout would not have sufficed, nor a threat and the order 'Let him not enter' when the council was entering. Yet I know that even a fine in money is judged by sensible people less painful than imprisonment.

'But he simply had to be imprisoned.' Very well, but for one hour or two, or, if you like, twice that, as was done in earlier times, if it ever happened that one of the councillors suffered this; and even that much seemed long, and generally releases came before imprisonment, as those who intervened forestalled entry into the jail.

And this was for crimes; but here what could one find? Nothing. For even if this man did become an informant to Lucianus of what was said or done in the court, he was not carrying out secrets, nor things that ought to have been kept silent, but what anyone could know, since the clerks sang them out in the colonnade.

And he did this and broke the laws not because he hated the man as wicked, nor as clumsy in the courts, nor as bad towards himself, but as good towards me and surpassing my household servants in his attentions to me.

Because of this, even if he had not been wholly blameless, he deserved to meet with leniency, at least from this man. For he knew that he was close to me and enjoyed my care. And he was also one of those who had done him some service, so that he could not retreat into ignorance of the man's familiarity with me. For he himself, before insulting me, had attributed the help that the man gave him to the man's gratitude towards me, saying this not to someone else but to me myself.

And moreover Callimachus, who lives in this council but was being harassed by the more august one and asked not to suffer this, since the law did not require it either, he did not wish to relieve of this injustice, although he had the power to do so by a letter, because I wished it so much. For this Callimachus is one of those who have studied with us, and besides his ability as a speaker he is well regarded for his character. So, avoiding the means by which he could have pleased me, he acted through those by which he knew he would hurt me.

And why need one dwell on these things? Well, the disease of the joints attacked me, and I had a vein cut, and sleep was nowhere to be had, an evil no less than the disease. And he himself was not unaware of this. How could he be, when his son was with me for his studies and there was every necessity for the boy to tell him what was done each day? So the one would have told him the reason for getting no [lesson], and the other heard it.

What, then, did he do on hearing it? Did he cry out as people in distress cry out, and send one of the couriers to find out how I was? No, he sent neither any of his other servants nor those who carry the boy's books. So far was he from [sending] the attendant. But the disease allowed me to return to my teaching when the eighth day had passed, and he was no better, but did not even send someone to say that he rejoiced at this very fact, that we were back in our classes.

Let it be observed also from what came next. And what is it that came next? My right hand was seized by the same disease more than before, so that the doctors, giving up trying to help me, looked at one another in despair; and he knew what a bad state I was in, as before, but sent nobody. But when his associates blamed him and said that he was doing wrong in appearing such in such circumstances, pushed and prodded, he did what he did not want to do. He sends his son to say anything rather than what suited the situation. After that neither the boy came nor those whose job is running.

And yet every day many feet brought many [messengers] from the others, both inviting him and complaining that he did not come, and this did not make his office any smaller; but if anyone had been sent to me, it would have been cast down at once and trampled underfoot, and would not have been what it was.

And yet he says: 'I myself wanted to come to you and was prevented by you.' But he did not want to; he said he did. And proofs that he did not want to are the things he left undone, which were far smaller. For one who thought me not worthy even of those, how could he think me worthy of something so great? Often, then, going to the hippodrome for the chariot races, he passed my doors, and though he saw the roof above the columns and knew that I was lying there groaning, shut off from food and from what is dearest to me, my speeches, he did not deign to make an enquiry befitting a friend about a friend, nor pray to hear better news. And yet he would have been at my house in five steps. But he did not want the city to know this, and he sent neither anything nor any of his more honoured staff nor those who have the whips in their hands.

Then, after letting three days pass, he sends one of those ivory writing-tablets, asking that he be given leave to walk over to me, knowing that I would not permit it, but wanting to have the reputation of having wished it. But I was not unaware of what he was thinking, and, keeping to my own rules, I did not permit it.

This much, however, I did know: that he would not have come even if I had invited him. For if he wanted to, what need was there to write such things? Why seek to hear from me, about something in his own power, whether he should do it? Or was there a fear that the hands of his soldiers would be overcome by the hands of my doorkeeper? Musonius knew what view I hold on such matters and how burdensome it is to me to be honoured in such ways. But nevertheless he came without any notice, using deeds instead of words. For he wanted to come; he did not claim to want to.

But, I suppose, this was all a game and an occasion for laughter for those who spend most of the night with him in witticisms and unjust pleasantries, in which someone has to suffer harm. One might learn that this is so from the following too. He was leaving after hearing a recital of verse, and when he learned later that he had passed me as I was enjoying the cool somewhere near there, away from the sun, he said he had been wronged by those who had not told him this at once; for he would have gone down to where I happened to be sitting and not have neglected the honour of doing so. But the man who said this then, later, after hearing an orator, did not on leaving look for the one whom he claimed he had been wronged in not seeing then.

Yet nevertheless he says that, though he loves, he is not loved. Very loving indeed was his treatment of poor Domninus, who was beaten, who was put in chains, who was deprived of the rights the laws give, among them an advocate. And his years did not even allow him to be sued, but nevertheless he was condemned and detained and made to pay, and called upon the laws in vain. Then, when those who pitied the young man begged him to quench his anger, he promised, but he remained the same. When those who had been deceived [pleaded again], there were other promises, but not even so did he check his anger. The reason is that he knows I would wish the orphan saved, since he is the child of friends and no idle member of my chorus.

As for Romulus, a man of my own age, poor after being well off and from a once prosperous house, I helped him, asking that he not be deprived here of his customary [relief] from previous governors; and he, persuaded and granting this fine favour, then changed sides and joins those warring against Romulus; and when Romulus demanded a trial on the matters he was charging, he ordered the attendants to shove him and show him lying on the ground; but they were more humane, and did the one thing, they shoved, but did not add the other.

Yet nevertheless he expects to be thought to have surpassed, in his honours to me, what was done by his predecessors. But he does not let Romulus off from being compelled again to send grain by ship, which was impossible given the poverty pressing on him. And yet he heard plainly that compulsion over this would not get the grain sent any the more, but would bring me with the greatest dishonour to Italy under false accusation, on the pretext that I was practising divination against the emperor's house, wanting to know what it was right not to know. And I added that, even if I came out alive, the journey itself was more dreadful to me than death.

So I asked him to follow the examples of all who had released Romulus because of his extreme poverty. He, yielding with difficulty and stopping the collection under pressure and ending the compulsion, imposed it again at once the next day, as if he had used the night as his adviser. And the second treatment was much harsher than the first. For the first was hearing threats from attendants; the second was standing in the court, being pelted by the judge's shouts, and having his back under the hands of the torturers.

And there was another affair before this, in which again the torturers [appear]. A mime, wanting to be frightening to the greengrocers so that he might get money when he asked for it, let loose a malicious remark against them. And he, using the despicable mime as his instructor in these matters as though he were a gentleman, made a night-hunt for the sellers of these goods, handing over the shaking-down to the soldiers. When their overseer, a member of the city council, called me to his aid, I came. And how could I not, when there were no wrongs done, or, if they erred even a little, the times bore the blame?

Those at the doors hoped that my mere appearance would at once stop what was frightening them; but he, though I was already inside, brought in the councillor with shouts that shake the heart. And again the torturers' right hands were over his neck. This would have been something new, done first by you, if anyone else had come to help; but the man who had provoked your anger was I, the one being honoured. With me sitting beside you, you exposed the chests and shoulders and backs and bellies of wretched men, and, laying them out, you carded them with whips, a thing unbearable to me even in dreams, so that, dizzy, with heart leaping, I put my right hand to [my eyes].

Such were the favours he did my eyes and ears; and as I was carried out, he let fly words against me full of abuse, rivalling what had been said before I came in. About both of these I learned later from one of his intimates, who both informed me and advised me neither to visit him often nor to expect to obtain anything.

As for Julian, whose interests I have never stopped caring for, by ruining them how did he not also ruin mine, in that I could do no good? For my wish was plain to everyone, I suppose. This man, then, who had spent the small fortune he had on the chariot races, and had been appointed manager of affairs by no obscure office, some of which he had to attend to in the city and some going round the countryside, this man, I say, he himself drove out, with no accusers indicting him and no facts taking the place of their voices, but because that man, long ill-treated by this one, did not keep silent. And he did not consider within himself that I would not bear such things easily, nor that I had often said to him that I would like the man to prosper.

Have I then been honoured by this too? Or by what happened to the son of Byzus? A man insulted him in anger, but when sober reproached himself, and, using the right given by the laws, on terms agreed beyond all telling, asked that the charge be dropped and that there be no one compelling him to prosecute. But he said, 'No, prosecute twice over, even if you do not want to,' wishing to get the young man into his hands. What did I not say then? What means of entreaty did I leave out, not rescuing a wrongdoer, but so that he might not suffer harm unjustly? But he persisted, warring against the law and putting his own desire before that man's humanity.

A fine honour indeed, and besides it this one. I asked him to free from grain transport the ship of the philosopher, a man like the gods and in their company, and to grant him the favour through me, though he himself, by the gods, had not asked me to request the favour. He had done this for many, owing to an abundance of ships, people not at all better than us. But this ship, it seems, carried the salvation of the emperor and the soldiers and the greatest cities above all others, and there was a danger that he would no longer have his head. For it was not I who should have asked for the release, but another of those who keep him in servitude through flattery.

And indeed for Domninus the sophist this would have made valid the honour voted to him by his fellow citizens of Chalcis. But as it is, what would have been just and fine and reasonable if it had found support from someone else became unjust and shameful and unreasonable since it was going to bring me some pleasure.

That my guess is not wrong one might learn from this. Some men once broke out of the prison, using the iron on their bodies, with the night helping them, and turned to banditry. They attacked travellers, and the governor laid the blame on those in charge of the door. But they showed themselves blameless, so that there was no room for punishment. There was another governor and another trial, and it was agreed that the deed had not been ventured in collusion with the guards.

This man came third to what had already been judged, and did so with no authority at all, just as the second had none either. The men he was going after, thinking I had some standing with him, came and begged me, and I at once [begged] him. But he made a tragedy of the breakout and of what those men had done, and of how they behaved outrageously in letters, and of how the escape had been arranged for the accursed men by the guards. So, with my powerlessness exposed, they took refuge with someone else. He did not need many words: the fear was dispelled, and the guards, who knew nothing of the bandits, got themselves off.

51. Yet he says he has made me great. Where, ever? When he was destroying Monimus the councillor, my pupil and the father of a pupil, with blows from the lead-weighted whips? So with these you made me great and enviable, using blows to my grief, blows from which [you said] the bodies of councillors need not be kept free. At these I went away with my head covered, thinking that I myself had received the blows, even if it was Monimus who was carried by the doctors to the bath. Those who heal such things, then, need no ally.

52. Yes, by Zeus, but in his dealings with Eusebius the sophist, a man I consider no less worthy to be called a sophist, he has made his defence for what was done to Monimus. But even if his relations with Eusebius were not bad, he would have shown his insolence by these acts: stirring up a prefect's decision, bringing back to the beginning what had reached its end, and calling to battle on behalf of men who had not the least need of a contest. And yet he ought to have had the more dignified letters read, then asked me about Eusebius' influence, and then asked them whether they were not aware that they themselves had written four decrees about him.

Why, then, did he need to instruct them in things by which they would thwart the settlement of these matters? Why make both me and him ridiculous? Or was this the very thing being contrived, that we should become ridiculous? Will anyone, then, count this an honour? And what of that, is it an honour to throw me out of the court with mockery?

For he wanted me to leave, as one who did not like seeing me, but he avoided saying outright that I would oblige him by leaving; putting forward the journey and the need to take up the business at once, he hurried me into calling for the hands that would carry me through, and I was outside the gates, thinking to honour him with what is customary on such an occasion. But he stayed and had his lunch, and after drinking went to sleep. I was worn out, and the Sun was not far from the streams of Ocean. So, exhausted as my exhausted servants were, I groaned, until someone, pitying what was happening, told [me] of the lunch and the sleep. So I went away in none too good health.

55. But in the matter of Diphilus, the son of Danaus the schoolmaster who has educated many young men, and who, doing the same as his father, surpasses his father in also being a good poet, have I been honoured in this? How he uprooted him from Palestine, though he needed nothing, by promising theatres and the gold from them, and how, having brought him to Cilicia, he brought him back without any help from himself, silent, having merely counted the cities and worn out by the daily expense, this I shall pass over.

But once, when I went in to him in the evening and described the poet's dejection, and how he thought himself wronged, hearing neither of two things, whether he should stay or whether he should leave, he, at a loss for any defence against this, for he was plainly in the wrong, said: "Well, I shall make him part of the festival, and he will have the Leader of the Muses as his listener at Daphne."

This too was painful for Diphilus, to have the suburb instead of the city, yet he let me persuade him to bear it, and he expected an invitation by letter to Daphne after Seleucia. But he, laughing at Diphilus and laughing at me, made himself available to other verses which he had previously avoided. Diphilus was nowhere, and nor was I. For he thought it terrible if Diphilus should be able to say in Palestine that I had some power, such as to help a friend. Diphilus, then, went away saying that he would not neglect the justice which he knows is owed him; for me it is enough to show all mankind that in this too I was dishonoured.

What came after this no one needs to learn from me, for no one is unaware of it. How could they be, of things displayed and noised abroad in public? More insolent than these are the things at home, since there was greater licence there. It is better for me to keep silent about them.

59. Yet he both says and swears that he loves me, and that he falls short of no one in this, and not even of those thought exceedingly [...] to think his hatred to be? But I know that friends advance the interests of friends, and do not pull them down, and try to make great things out of small, not small out of great; but he has left out nothing that tends to this. And thanks to the gods he was not able to do as much as he wished, but he made it plain that he wished more than he was able.

Yet he says he loves me above everyone, and that in his intention he surpasses nature, and he swears to it, doing an old thing, perjuring himself, as though the gods were very far from the earth and knew nothing of what is done or said on it. That this is so, one might learn from this.

For when the law came into force, by which others may not go to the governors' residences, and it prevailed and prevented entry, others' notes are carried there every day, letters taking the place of the tongue, but mine never. The reason is that to others he said they must send and get round the law, but to me he did not. And yet, even if I did not obey his first words, he ought to have compelled me with second and third, and to have kept up his eagerness to the end, with something even of threat, such as may arise from friendship. As it is, he seems to me to find fault with the law on account of others, but to admire it as far as I am concerned.

62. That he says he loves me but does the opposite, Romulus, dragged in again, shows. He knew that, once dragged in again, he would press hard on me. And yet it was the part of a friend not to wake an evil that was sleeping, but, if someone else should wake it, to put it to sleep. As it is, he has set biters around that man too, so that he would bite me. And this is done many times each day, my teaching of the young not being allowed to proceed in good order.

63. But tell me, is this the act of one who loves me, to avoid judging the case in which, because of the strength of my rights, he knew he would vote for me? And yet earlier he urged me to bring it in, and blamed the delay, and said that the laws were on our side.

But that was the act of a man doing something for himself, while this was done, once that had been accomplished, out of his hatred for me. While seeking that, he deceived; having got it, he did not let [the case proceed], but laid plots and, robbing me of the victory that was certain to follow, so as to gratify his flatterers, he led the case to the point where it was silenced by the month [running out].

65. He heard that it was proper to release a man wrongly imprisoned, who was going to be of benefit to the council. He did not release him. Why? Because the one who mentioned the prisoner was I. Had the same words been spoken by someone else, he would have been released, if the speaker were not, as I am, useless to Eustathius' affairs.

66. There was, as he supposed, a favour even in his threatening to plot against Thalassius. And the pretext was very reasonable: that Thalassius, having control of the speeches of mine that had been shown, did not give them to him when he asked, keeping up his thirst. But he never thirsted for them at all, but wished to seem to, perhaps thinking he would gain something toward reputation, as with his son too. Saying that he would at one time bring him, at another send for him, at another send him, as if to better streams, he kept him in Tyre and among inferior studies, as he himself called them, until the office summoned the young man here with his brothers.

And indeed, if he had [them], he did not thirst for my speeches, by his own account, and if he did not have them, he did not desire them. For how would he not have had them, if he wished? Why then did he need to play games and, pretending to love what he despised, insult with threats a noble man, who fears the gods, respects his friends, is just and temperate, master of his tongue and master of his pleasures, who pities flatterers, being so far from flattery, and who defends himself with silence against those who live by abuse?

You asked for the parchment, not so as to have its contents copied out, but so as [to have] that very [copy] itself. Yet this is not the mark of a lover, not to value his beloved even at a stater. What wrong, then, did he do in not giving it to one who would not give it back? And to wish to acquire in this way even things of little account would be the mark of just anybody.

69. As for what you are toward me, it has been shown by what I have said, even if much has been left out, but it will be clear from this too. For you live with those who have been convicted of wickedness in corrupting what is due to their teacher: you keep company with them, spend your time with them, converse with them, dine with them, drink with them, lunch with them, and if they wish to sleep there, they have full licence and nothing prevents it. And the talk on each of these occasions is directed against my character, containing nothing sound, but much pleasure for both parties, the liars and the listener.

And whatever those men decide must prevail, even if I want the opposite. For they have no children, but much gold, the fruit of inherited wickedness, and Fate knows how to carry off the younger before the elder. So with this attentiveness he is buying himself a will to his own advantage. To such a hunter, who thinks everything of less worth than money, my interest is naturally 'of no account'.

Why then does he not admit this and make his defence on these grounds, but expects, while insulting me openly, to persuade [people] that he has not ceased to honour me? He who yesterday did the same thing through his doorkeeper, who shares many of his secrets and imitates his master. For when that burglar received a letter of mine complaining of the unjust imprisonment of a mother and her daughter, he drove away the man who delivered the letter, saying that it was not mine but belonged to the one who had delivered it.

Such he made my servants out to be in his story, slandering my life with their audacities, whether I was unaware of them or aware. And yet to invent such things is no wrong if one means to undo some wrong. But all the same, [the letter] was in fact from the one it was said to be from, from me, who share the distress of the wronged and am struck by their misfortunes no less than they are.

73. And old Eusebius, who has often sung of his release 'tomorrow' but has not yet obtained it in fact, what do you think he will reveal? Is it not that my speeches on his behalf became harmful to him, while others have been released who took refuge with other men, whose servants go there carrying baskets and hampers, which hold fish for that most just of men, and the produce of the trees?

74. Now another thing, no less. Coming into the council chamber to enlarge the council according to the present law, he did not call me, though he knew from close at hand that I was sitting near by in a place not my own, and that although [the city] had for a long time seen this partnership of the governors, who roused the council whenever it slept. He ought, then, to have used this practice and not brought back what had been [neglected], and he had many fine arguments, had he wished to do something just. But as it was, he thought it equally proper for me, who can list countless ancestors who served as councillors, to be absent as for those who come from I know not where. And it seems to me that he would gladly have called some of them while passing me over, had he not feared the excess of the insult.

75. Again, when he was asked for the same favour which he had often promised and never once given, he cleverly, as he thought, put it off by asking in return for speeches of mine, praises of himself, no doubt, knowing that I would not deliver them, for many reasons, but providing a pretext for not having granted the favour so often slighted. And so in word he made himself a lover of these speeches, since in truth he had no regard for my speeches at all. If he had, the ten months would have been spent on them, and not on the people on whom they are now spent, whom everyone knows. On their knees and in their hands is continually that ridiculous offspring, the [speeches] that were displayed, cherished even above those of Plato.

As for this present business, the great love and the claim to be distressed at not getting [a speech], it is not love; rather, a man worth much to litigants through the strength of his art, who married from the house of these people and thinks it proper to do them good, seeing him carried off elsewhere and neglecting those he ought not to neglect, pushed him, very unwillingly, into these words: that I must, I must get a speech, and that I would suffer terribly if I did not get one.

What he wanted, then, was those things; what he has been forced into is this. And it is not right to count this as his rather than as the doing of the man who forced him, unless he could persuade [us] of this, that he was asleep this whole time. But he was not asleep; he was among the people he was among, having cast his vote in public that all [my] speeches had been refuted.

78. And he will say that this alone would have saved Romulus. Why? For even if this does not come to you, other things surely have. Among them are the things your son has acquired from us and possesses, which are great and seem so to you yourself, and which have often roused you from your bed. Should the favour not, then, have been given for these, even if there was nothing more to gain? Or would you say this to a champion who reminded you of a reward, too, that he would receive it for a second feat of valour, but that what he had done was not yet worthy of honour?

'When he has spoken, you will give.' What then? Have I not spoken already? Or are the things spoken then nothing, and the things done because of what was spoken, which eclipsed all the frenzy of all theatres? Then you admitted that you had been honoured as by no one else; but now, as though you would be giving in return for nothing, if you did give, you expect to receive first, if you are to give. And yet, if you are grateful for those things, proceed to the repayment; but if you think them small and nothing, it is no wonder if you will think these too to be nothing, so that I would not be surprised if even after receiving you will not give.

As for your oaths, you yourself have stripped them of credit by the number of oaths you have disregarded, so that even someone who buys justice from you while you swear cannot be confident, but is afraid that the horn may not follow what has been sworn. So here too there is fear that you will avoid giving in your turn, and having received, will sing and mock.

81. And if I must mention something else, in return for which something ought to have come to me from him: of the things he wrote, and they were nonsense, I heard many before this governorship, and many during it, pieces meant to torment, for that is how he began. My ears were wounded by them, but I had to bear it and, worst of all, to praise them too. So he had no need to ask anything else of me, since I had done him things worthy of gratitude.

But he did nothing good for us either before or after, since even the lawsuit itself, by whose judgment I would have escaped an unjust penalty, he neither brought into court nor tried, seeing both the number and the standing of my opponents. For they had no just claim, but they were many. Their being many is frightening to an authority that is sick, but not to one that is healthy. And at the same time he had no regard for me, convinced as he was that he composed fine speeches.
83. Such is this noble fellow toward us. He is indignant that when his governorship ended we did not fall down and weep. But, it seems, this should have been done when he was entering upon it.
